findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: £88m of the £109.946m capital programme (80%) depends on unproven business cases for three regeneration schemes
findings.detail: Three major projects are included in the capital plan: York Place (£18.136m), Midway Carpark (£36.350m), and Aparthotel on Ryecroft (£33.712m). Each is explicitly marked 'subject to the business case that is currently being developed'. Together they represent £88m of planned spend. If any fail approval, the council has material borrowing exposure with no offsetting capital receipts to repay it.
findings.matters: Regeneration schemes deliver the capital receipts needed to fund the capital programme and pay down borrowing; if business cases fail, the council carries unplanned debt

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut funding by £964k in 2026/27, a structural loss not fully resolved
findings.detail: The council receives £9.360m in 2025/26 from Business Rates Retention and grants subject to Fair Funding Review redistribution. This drops to £8.396m in 2026/27 — a £964k structural cut. The council set aside £500k in the prior year, leaving £464k of this loss unfunded in the budget gap. Recovery is not expected until 2028/29.
findings.matters: Structural funding losses of nearly £1m cannot be closed by one-off savings and require sustained service reductions or efficiency gains — a material ongoing pressure
findings.figures: £9.360m (2025/26) → £8.396m (2026/27), £964k loss, £464k gap remaining after prior-year provision

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Housing supply assumption of 3,718 properties over five years underpins council tax base growth, but borough has 'low levels of house building'
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes the housing market supply requirement of 3,718 properties over five years will be met per the trajectory in the draft Local Plan, thus increasing the tax base accordingly. However, the document notes that the borough has 'in recent decades it has seen low levels of house building which have not kept up with housing demand,' and this affordability gap is driving pressure on homelessness and temporary accommodation services.
findings.matters: If the draft Local Plan trajectory for house building is not met, council tax base growth assumptions fail, worsening future-year budget gaps. The affordability gap also signals demand pressure on services.
findings.figures: 3,718 properties assumed over 5-year period
findings.quote: Newcastle-under-Lyme has a growing population, but in recent decades it has seen low levels of house building which have not kept up with housing demand. findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031

findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement will increase from £19.893m (31 March 2025) to £31.278m by 2028/29, an increase of £11.385m over three years. The document states 'significant capital receipts are expected' but gives no timeline or certainty.
findings.matters: The quantum of new borrowing (£67.95m including regeneration) is substantial and contingent on capital receipts that are not quantified. Slippage in receipts or external contributions would require additional PWLB borrowing or repriorisation.
findings.figures: CFR: £19.893m (31.3.25) → £31.278m (by 2028/29). Capital programme £109.946m. Borrowing (standard + regeneration) £67.95m over four years.

findings.detail: The forecast Business Rates reserve balance falls from £2.675m (31 March 2026) to £1.445m (31 March 2027). findings.matters: Reorganisation costs are a sign of institutional change; if the reorganisation proceeds, transition costs could escalate, and if it does not, the budget benefit of the assumed nil allocation in 2028/29 will not materialise.
findings.quote: A small number of new pressures facing the Council in 2026/27 have also been provided for, these include an allowance for costs associated with Local Government Re-organisation amounting to £0.400m (decreasing to £0.200m in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29).

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns significant budget risks mean reserves will need to be called on.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's statutory report identifies specific risks that could derail the budget: spending exceeding budget, income falling short (especially capital receipts from major capital schemes), and changes to government funding. Officer explicitly flags that reserves will need to be drawn on if these risks materialize.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess reserve adequacy and budget resilience. Finance directors need to plan for potential drawdowns and ensure reserves are sufficient for the identified risks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Housing affordability pressures are creating unquantified demand on homelessness and temporary accommodation services with risk to council tax income
findings.detail: The document notes that low housing supply relative to demand and the cost-of-living crisis are creating affordability pressures on residents. This is pushing demand for homelessness and temporary accommodation services, which are typically high-cost, unpredictable services. The MTFS does not separately quantify this emerging pressure, and the document acknowledges the risk of dampening council tax income from residents struggling with affordability.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted demand for high-cost services (homelessness, temp accommodation) can create in-year pressure; falling council tax income from households struggling with affordability directly hits a core funding source.
findings.figures: Housing affordability ratio 6.1 (lower than England average 7.7 but indicates pressure); population increase 3.8% but housing supply not kept pace; pressure noted as existing but not separately costed
findings.quote: The resulting affordability gap for residents influenced by the cost of living puts pressure on our homelessness and temporary accommodations services but also has the risk of dampening council tax income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced on £1.752m of identified savings, with £638k being a one-off staffing restructuring
findings.detail: The council has identified £1.752m of savings for 2026/27 to meet the funding gap, but the composition is concerning: £638k is staffing-related (appearing in 2026/27 only, suggesting one-off restructuring); £474k is described as 'Other Financing' without explanation; the remainder is from tax base growth and council tax increases. Delivery of these savings is not certain.
findings.matters: If savings are not realised—particularly the £638k one-off restructuring or the unexplained £474k—the budget will run into deficit in-year, requiring emergency reserves or further cuts.
findings.figures: Savings target: £1.752m for 2026/27; Staffing-related: £638k (2026/27 only); Other Financing: £474k (2026/27 only); Tax base: £308k; Council Tax increase: £179k; Good housekeeping: £66k; Income generation: £87k
findings.quote: To date savings of £1.752m have been identified for 2026/27 enabling a balanced position to be proposed.

findings.headline: Collection fund deficit from previous years will be repaid in 2026/27, eroding Business Rates reserve by £1.230m
findings.detail: A collection fund deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 must be repaid in 2026/27. This causes the Business Rates reserve (which buffers against future collection losses) to fall from a forecast £2.675m at 31 March 2026 to £1.445m at 31 March 2027. This represents a one-time cash cost that reduces financial buffers.
findings.matters: Depletes the council's contingency for business rates volatility or the Fair Funding Review varying from estimates; a smaller reserve means less ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: Business Rates reserve: £2.675m (31.3.26) → £1.445m (31.3.27); repayment reducing the reserve by approximately £1.230m
findings.quote: A deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 will be repayable by the Council in 2026/27 – the reduced forecast balance at 31 March 2027 of the reserve reflects this repayment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: £109.946m capital programme over three years requires significant borrowing of £56.565m, dependent on future capital receipts
findings.detail: The council is planning a large regeneration investment programme funded by external contributions (primarily Town Deals), capital receipts, and £56.565m of borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement will increase to £31.278m by 2027/28. Large capital receipts (£17m) are expected in 2028/29 but only modest receipts in 2026/27 and 2027/28, creating timing risk.
findings.matters: Substantial borrowing increases debt servicing costs and refinancing risk; delayed or reduced capital receipts could require additional borrowing or revenue cuts.

findings.quote: These schemes total £109.946m including major investment into the Borough via external funding in terms of the Town Deals Fund for both Newcastle and Kidsgrove and associated projects.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 reduces settlement funding by £0.964m in 2026/27 with only partial mitigation in place
findings.detail: The council's settlement funding subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review is forecast to fall from £9.360m in 2025/26 to £8.396m in 2026/27. Only £0.500m was set aside in 2025/26 to meet this, leaving a £0.464m gap in 2026/27 that must be addressed through other means.
findings.matters: A material reduction in a core funding source impacts borrowing capacity and financial resilience; the gap must be met by savings or drawdown of reserves.
findings.figures: £9.360m (2025/26) → £8.396m (2026/27), a reduction of £0.964m; £0.500m set aside, leaving £0.464m gap
findings.quote: As part of the 2025/26 budget setting £0.500m was set aside to contribute to this anticipated reduction, as such a gap of £0.464m remains and has been included as a pressure to be addressed for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Pension scheme membership moving into surplus; complex IFRS accounting required revised actuarial report with £1.869m impact
findings.detail: KPMG notes that market conditions mean many councils are finding pension surpluses growing and becoming material, requiring complex accounting under IFRS/SORP. Newcastle-under-Lyme's initial IAS 19 report (25 April 2025) showed variances that exceeded acceptable thresholds; a revised report (23 May 2025) was issued. Corrected misstatements totalling £1.869m were recorded related to asset remeasurement and employer contributions, reflecting the revised actuarial data.
findings.matters: Pension surplus recognition involves complex accounting with high estimation uncertainty. A late actuarial revision forcing corrected misstatements suggests the initial actuary work or council review was inadequate. Lenders care about the materiality and reliability of pension asset/liability positions.
findings.figures: Corrected misstatement - remeasurement gain/loss increase £1.869m; employer contributions increase £257k; benefits adjustment £132k
findings.quote: Also, recent changes to market conditions have meant that more councils are finding themselves moving into surplus in their Local Government Pension Scheme (or surpluses have grown and have become material). The requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement.

findings.headline: Valuation working papers contained formula errors and unused data inputs not caught by management review
findings.detail: On receipt of workings supporting asset valuations, KPMG identified formula errors in key assumptions and relevant data provided by finance (e.g., cashflows) that had not been appropriately applied. This evidenced lack of formal review by management. KPMG recommended formal review of significant valuation workings, particularly those reliant on finance team inputs. Management responded that valuations will continue to be formally reviewed each year.
findings.matters: Management bears ultimate responsibility for valuations in the financial statements despite relying on internal valuers. Unreviewed working papers with formula errors suggest control gaps. This is particularly material given the Castle Car Park (£12m) was valued on investment method during the year.
findings.figures: Issues found in workings for two specific assets; Castle Car Park construction cost £12m, valued at existing use value using investment method
findings.quote: On receipt of the workings to support the valuation of two specific assets, we identified formula errors for key assumptions in the valuation. Similarly, relevant data inputs had been provided by finance (e.g cashflows) which had not been appropriately applied to elements of the workings evidencing a lack of review by management over the valuation workings.

findings.headline: £630k in uncorrected audit misstatements not adjusted in the financial statements
findings.detail: KPMG identified three uncorrected misstatements totalling £630k: £255k York Place investment property (inappropriate revenue capitalisation mixed with capital spend); £885k pension assets (returns variance); and £896k Ryecroft land (should be asset held for sale, not PPE). KPMG notes these have no effect on the audit opinion individually or in aggregate, but formally requested adjustment under ISA 450.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements, however small individually, represent errors in the financial statements. Accumulation across years creates risk. Lenders review audit findings to assess financial statement reliability; uncorrected items suggest either weak controls or disputed valuations.
findings.figures: Total uncorrected misstatements £630k (0.3% of assets, 0.4% of reserves); Investment property error £255k; Pension error £885k; Land reclassification £896k
findings.quote: The aggregated surplus impact of unadjusted audit differences would be £0.2m. In line with ISA 450 we request that you adjust for these items. However, they will have no effect on the opinion in the auditor's report, individually or in aggregate.

findings.headline: Journal entry approval controls inadequate: junior staff can approve entries from seniors, with undocumented review precision
findings.detail: KPMG's detailed ISA 315(R) evaluation of controls found the ledger system permits approval of journals by team members more junior than the poster. Review precision prior to approval is not sufficiently documented to enable audit reliance as a manual control. KPMG could not rely on segregation of duties in journal entry processing, though management considers controls proportionate to risk.
findings.matters: Inadequate journal entry controls create fraud and error risk. This is a core financial reporting control responding to a significant audit risk. Lenders need confidence that material entries are properly reviewed and authorized.
findings.figures: 9 high-risk journal entries identified; no issues found in those tested
findings.quote: Under the requirements of ISA315r, we conduct a detailed evaluation of the design and implementation of controls around journal entries. This identified that the ledger system permits approval of journals by team members that are more junior than the poster.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only £26.3m of £51.3m planned spend; recurring underspend raises forecasting credibility
findings.detail: The mid-year revised capital budget of £51.3m achieved only £26.3m expenditure (£25.1m under). This follows a prior-year £44m underspend. KPMG notes: 'following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively.' Much relates to externally funded projects.
findings.matters: Repeated material underspends suggest either poor forecasting capability or difficulty executing schemes. For lenders, this indicates potential project delivery risk and questions the reliability of capital planning. For finance officers, it damages credibility in budget setting.
findings.figures: Capital budget £51.3m revised; actual spend £26.3m; underspend £25.1m; prior year underspend £44m
findings.quote: Whilst the underspend was much improved on the prior year (£44m underspend in 23-24), following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively.

findings.headline: Pension liability decreased by £22.1m but with £885k uncorrected valuation error accumulated over prior years
findings.detail: The council's Local Government Pension Scheme liability fell 13.8% due to actuarial gains from changed assumptions. However, KPMG identified an £885k uncorrected misstatement in pension asset valuation, driven by differences between actual investment returns and the actuary's estimates; this accumulated a prior-year £293k uncorrected misstatement. The actuary's control review lacks precision and documentation sufficient for audit reliance.
findings.matters: Material balance sheet movements driven by estimates create valuation risk, and uncorrected misstatements accumulating over years suggests control gaps. Lenders need confidence in pension liability accuracy given its size relative to council finances.
findings.figures: Pension liability decreased £22.1m (13.8% reduction); uncorrected pension asset misstatement £885k; prior-year carry-forward £293k
findings.quote: Following this update, all variances fell within acceptable threshold. This misstatement is driven by the differences between actual returns and those estimated by the actuary. This resulted in an unadjusted audit difference of £293k in the prior year, accumulating to £885k in 2024-25.

findings.headline: Castle Car Park £12m capital investment now operational and valued using investment method based on income forecasts, introducing new estimation risk
findings.detail: The council completed construction of the Castle Car Park at £12m during 2024/25 and reclassified it from Asset Under Construction to operational land and buildings. It is being valued at existing use value using the investment method, which depends on forecasted rental income and yield assumptions. This introduces new estimation uncertainty as the valuation relies entirely on assumptions about income-generation potential.
findings.matters: Material capital investment now depends on commercial income forecasts; if rental income underperforms assumptions, both valuation and recoverable asset value are at risk; signals council pursuing revenue-generation strategies dependent on market performance.
findings.figures: £12m capital cost; reclassified from AUC to operational; land and buildings balance sheet movement £2.2m (primarily this reclassification)
findings.quote: However, during the year, the Council has completed the construction of the Castle Car Park at a cost of £12m. This will be valued at its existing use value (EUV) using the investment method (based on its income potential).

findings.headline: Valuation working papers for significant assets contained formula errors and lacked formal management review of key assumptions
findings.detail: The auditors identified formula errors in the working papers supporting valuation of two specific assets. Additionally, data inputs provided by finance (e.g. cashflows) were not appropriately applied to elements of calculations, evidencing lack of management review. An absence of formal control reviewing assumptions adopted by valuers was noted, which directly responds to the significant audit risk over land and buildings valuation.
findings.matters: Material asset valuations (land and buildings £43.2m at prior year-end, £37.6m valued at depreciated replacement cost) are unreliable without proper review controls; directly increases risk of misstated balance sheet values.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £43.2m (prior year); £37.6m valued at DRC; investment property portfolio £13.5m (prior year)
findings.quote: On receipt of the workings to support the valuation of two specific assets, we identified formula errors for key assumptions in the valuation. Similarly, relevant data inputs had been provided by finance (e.g cashflows) which had not been appropriately applied to elements of the workings evidencing a lack of review by management over the valuation workings.

findings.headline: Pension asset valuation contained £885k uncorrected misstatement driven by actuary's return assumptions diverging significantly from actual
findings.detail: The council's IAS 19 actuarial valuation required revision from the initial 25 April 2025 report to a revised 23 May 2025 report after variances with actual benefits paid and contributions exceeded acceptable thresholds. The auditors identified a £885k uncorrected misstatement in pension assets, primarily because the actuary's estimated return rate diverged materially from actual administrator returns. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was not corrected.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material to council balance sheet (£137.6m); audit uncertainty about valuation methodology and actuary assumptions indicates control gap; uncorrected misstatements accumulating across years.
findings.figures: £885k uncorrected misstatement in 2024/25 (£293k prior year unadjusted); pension obligation £137.6m (down £22.1m year-on-year); pension assets £176.1m (up £2.6m)
findings.quote: This misstatement is driven by the differences between actual returns and those estimated by the actuary. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was uncorrected.

findings.headline: Capital programme underperformance continues: £25.1m underspent against £51.3m revised budget in 2024/25, following £44m underspend in 2023/24
findings.detail: The council began the year with a £59.9m capital programme of which £42.2m was delayed expenditure from 2023/24 when only 21% of budget was spent due to inflationary pressures. After mid-year review, the revised programme totalled £51.295m but actual expenditure reached only £26.3m. The auditors flag this persistent pattern as raising a 'risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively' and recommend more robust challenge and monitoring with clear communication of slippage.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend signals forecasting weakness and delivery risk on council priorities; for lenders, unreliable project forecasting and execution capability poses risk to cashflow and asset deployment.
findings.figures: £59.9m initial programme; £51.295m revised programme; £26.3m actual spend (£25.1m below plan); prior year £44m underspend from 21% budget execution rate
findings.quote: following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will create unquantified budget costs
findings.detail: The council has included a budget pressure for Local Government Reorganisation but explicitly states the cost is unknown. An estimate of £400k has been included for 2026/27 but is provisional. Confirmation of transitional arrangements and timing has not yet been received, creating uncertainty in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Unquantified risk to the MTFS that could worsen the budget gap if costs exceed estimates; timing and magnitude remain uncertain
findings.figures: £400k estimated for 2026/27 (explicitly uncertain)
findings.quote: In addition to the above, a budget pressure in respect of Local Government Reorganisation has been included in the MTFS. It is not yet known how much this will cost, therefore this will be closely monitored and updated.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £2.007m is assessed as fully committed to covering identified risks
findings.detail: A preliminary risk assessment indicates that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m is needed to provide sufficient cover for identified risks. This suggests reserves are already committed and cannot absorb additional pressures without either drawing on other reserves or requiring further savings.
findings.matters: Tight reserve position limits the council's financial flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures; any further deterioration would require immediate savings or borrowing
findings.figures: £2.007m General Fund reserve
findings.quote: A preliminary assessment suggests that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m will be required to provide sufficient cover for potential risks.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs forecast to escalate significantly in out-years as capital programme matures
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement is estimated to reach £42.490m by 2035/36. Borrowing revenue budget of £0.947m is increasing by £0.058m for 2026/27, with forecast costs spiking to £200k in 2029/30 and £535k in 2030/31, reflecting the growing debt service impact of the capital programme.
findings.matters: Growing debt service obligations will consume increasing amounts of future revenue budgets and reduce financial flexibility, particularly from 2029/30 onwards
findings.figures: Current budget £0.947m; increase £0.058m for 2026/27; £200k additional in 2029/30; £535k additional in 2030/31; total capital requirement £42.490m by 2035/36
findings.quote: The capital financing requirement is estimated to increase to £42.490m by 2035/36 based on the current capital programme and the revenue implications have been reflected in the revised MTFS. It is anticipated that the current borrowing revenue budget of £0.947m will need to be increased by £0.058m to provide for borrowing costs that may be incurred during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Budget gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 with savings proposals not due until December
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts a budget gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 and £3.069m over the five-year period. Detailed budget proposals including savings and investment plans are scheduled to be presented to Cabinet in December 2025, with final council approval in February 2026, creating a compressed timeline for meaningful scrutiny.
findings.matters: Material budget shortfall requiring significant savings or income generation; tight timeline increases risk of inadequate scrutiny or solutions
findings.quote: The current forecast around financial pressures facing the Council is for a gap in 2026/27 of £1.777m and over the 5-year period of the MTFS, £3.069m.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut government funding by £0.964m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Funding subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review drops from £9.360m (2025/26) to £8.396m (2026/27), a reduction of £0.964m. The council set aside £0.5m in 2025/26 to cushion part of this impact, leaving a £0.464m gap to be addressed in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Real, measurable loss of government funding that forms half of the overall budget gap and is locked in by central government policy
findings.quote: Funding received and retained by the Council in 2025/26 that is subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amounts to £9.360m, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 with no savings plan presented
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £1.777m gap in 2026/27 and £3.069m over the full five-year MTFS. The report states that work is underway to develop savings proposals to close this gap, but none are presented. Savings proposals are not due to Cabinet until December 2025, leaving a compressed timetable to identify and consult on £1.777m of cuts.
findings.matters: The council has not yet identified how it will balance its budget within a six-month window, and given the minimal reserves and escalating pressures, there is execution risk
findings.quote: The current forecast around financial pressures facing the Council is for a gap in 2026/27 of £1.777m and over the 5-year period of the MTFS, £3.069m.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £2.007m at minimum necessary level with no surplus capacity
findings.detail: A risk assessment of reserves concludes that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m is required just to cover assessed risks. This leaves no discretionary buffer to absorb unexpected expenditure, income shortfalls, or emergencies.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves mean the council cannot self-insure against forecast pressures, making it dependent on external funding or forced service cuts if actual spending exceeds budget
findings.figures: £2.007m General Fund reserve
findings.quote: A preliminary assessment suggests that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m will be required to provide sufficient cover for potential risks.

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement estimated at £42.490m by 2035/36; borrowing costs forecast to rise from £58k (2026/27) to £535k (2030/31)
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement is estimated to reach £42.490m by 2035/36. Borrowing costs are forecast to rise from £58k in 2026/27 to £200k in 2029/30 and £535k in 2030/31, representing a more than ninefold increase in annual debt servicing within a five-year window.
findings.matters: Growing capital commitments will create an expanding revenue drag, with the sharpest increases hitting in 2029/30 when other pressures may be acute. This constrains future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £42.490m capital financing requirement by 2035/36, borrowing costs £58k (2026/27), £200k (2029/30), £535k (2030/31)
findings.quote: The capital financing requirement is estimated to increase to £42.490m by 2035/36 based on the current capital programme and the revenue implications have been reflected in the revised MTFS.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut retained funding by £0.964m with only partial prior mitigation
findings.detail: When the Fair Funding Review redistributes accumulated business rates growth in 2026/27, the council's retained funding falls from £9.360m to £8.396m. Although £0.500m was set aside in 2025/26 to soften the blow, a gap of £0.464m remains unfunded, representing a real loss of resources from changes to the funding formula.
findings.matters: This is a permanent loss of income driven by central government policy, reducing baseline financial capacity at the same time the council faces other pressures
findings.quote: Funding received and retained by the Council in 2025/26 that is subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amounts to £9.360m, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs escalating with no solution, escalated to the Chancellor
findings.detail: The council faces continuing rising costs of temporary and supported accommodation, a statutory obligation for vulnerable and homeless residents. The Portfolio Holder has written directly to the Chancellor of the Exchequer requesting emergency funding. The cost pressure is not separately quantified in the MTFS, suggesting it is either unquantifiable or exceptionally large.
findings.matters: This is a legal obligation with uncontrollable cost drivers and the council is already seeking central government bailout, signalling they cannot contain it through normal savings
findings.figures: Cost not separately quantified
findings.quote: The continuing rising costs of temporary and supported accommodation that the Council is required to provide for vulnerable and homeless residents

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle-under-Lyme's 2026/27 budget has a £1.599m gap, and £4.649m over five years
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle-under-Lyme Borough Council's 2026/27 budget has a net base budget gap of £1.599m. The gap over the five years of its medium-term financial strategy is £4.649m, according to papers for the Audit and Standards Committee meeting on 16 November. The prior-year table gave the cumulative gap as £5.042m.

The council approved a £20m general fund budget for 2026/27 in February 2026. The strategy includes a £1.504m provision for cost increases in 2026/27 and £5.53m across 2026-31. It covers employers' National Insurance, an assumed 3% pay award, temporary accommodation and local government reorganisation costs. The papers say pay awards remain the largest pressure over the period, with reorganisation costs alongside them in the short term.

The council says it is mitigating the gap through reduced pension contributions and a widened tax base. The figures appear in two appendices to the committee papers: the auditor's annual report for 2025-26 and a separate risk assessment.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle-under-Lyme borrows £8m for first time in latest year, shifting from net lender to net debtor
news_drafts.lead: Newcastle-under-Lyme took on £8m of external debt during 2025/26 at a 5.4% average interest rate, marking its first external borrowing in the period and reversing its financial position from net lender to net debtor. At the end of March 2025, the council held no external debt and £3.05m in investments. By the end of March 2026, it held £8m in debt against £4.05m in investments, a £7m shift in its net position to borrowing of £3.95m. The shift reflects tighter treasury management: 87 of 88 investments were confined to periods of 2 weeks or less, and the council's capital programme delivered at 77% of budget, with £8.3m of planned spending not deployed.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle-under-Lyme faces £777k budget gap with no contingency reserve
news_drafts.lead: Newcastle-under-Lyme faces a budget gap of £777,000 in 2027/28. The council's general fund reserve — money set aside for unexpected costs — stands at £2.225 million and is fully required to cover financial risks, leaving no extra cushion. A preliminary risk assessment concludes the reserve will be needed "in full to provide sufficient cover for potential risks". The gap is forecast to widen to £1.47 million over five years. The council is pursuing commercial opportunities including commercial waste services and property investment to generate income to address the shortfall. Savings proposals are due to Cabinet in December.
